interactions.summary: A student objects that the return-to-God model makes life itself puzzling, another student says God wanted relationship because he was lonely, and Jiang accepts that answer as the opening to his next question.
A student misreads Jiang as saying plants and animals are closer to God because of obedience to natural law, and Jiang sharply reverses that by saying they lack souls altogether.
interactions.speaker_attribution: student question followed by Jiang correction

interactions.summary: Jiang returns to Dante's resurrection line, a student glosses it as the soul's immortality, and Jiang radicalizes that reading by saying humans are really an aspect of God and therefore cannot truly die.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang with student gloss and expansion

claims.claim: A student challenges Jiang's framework by asking why life is necessary at all if the soul already wants to return to God.
A student answers that God created Adam because God wanted relationship and was lonely.
Jiang rejects the idea that animals and plants are spiritually closer to God because they obey natural law, arguing instead that they do not have souls.
Jiang reiterates that the universe and evolution produce human bodies, but what makes humans unique is the soul, the part of God placed into them.
Jiang says the soul always desires to return to the whole, whether or not humans know this, and treats that desire as their truest aspiration.
A student glosses Dante's resurrection line as the Christian claim that the soul is immortal even if the flesh is corrupt.
Jiang interprets resurrection to mean that what humans really are is an aspect of God, so death is not annihilation but rebirth.
Jiang contrasts Dante's framework with modern teachings that the purpose of life is wealth, longevity, and bodily survival, implying those goals miss the point if death is inevitable.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang snaps the class back by declaring that plants and animals do not possess souls at all.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The blunt refusal stops the discussion from confusing lawful obedience with the human divine spark.

signature_moments.moment: What you think is your identity as a body is displaced by a more radical identity as an aspect of God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: what you are really is an aspect of god
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's strongest anthropological claim and the basis for Jiang's reading of resurrection.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang drains fear from death by recoding it as inevitable rebirth rather than extinction.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can't possibly die you can only be reborn
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a doctrinal point into an existential provocation aimed at modern anxieties about survival.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's formulation for the soul's deepest aspiration as a separated part seeking reunion with God.
Jiang's description of the soul as what humans most fundamentally are, grounding eternity and rebirth.
Jiang's existential gloss on resurrection: death does not erase the soul because the soul is divine in origin.

chronology_notes.note: The packet turns the soul model into an existential argument: after clarifying that natural obedience is not the human distinction, Jiang reads resurrection as proof that bodily death cannot be the final horizon of life.

uncertainty_notes.note: The loneliness-and-relationship answer comes from students rather than Jiang, and Jiang does not fully develop or defend it inside this packet.
